results.title: Nebius raises GPU prices 17–21% effective… · Slicast
highlights:
# Nebius raises GPU prices 17–21% effective today; second price increase in three months; NBIS/IREN/CRWV gain in sync

Trade press Slicast · September 30, 2026 at 21:01 UTC · Global · Source: Yahoo Finance

N ebius is raising prices on its GPU compute resources effective October 1, marking the second price increase in three months as the company scales its global AI infrastructure and secures additional financing tied to deployed capacity.

The price hikes affect Nvidia's latest processors. H100 GPUs will rise 17% to $4.50 per GPU-hour from $3.85. H200 pricing increases 20% to $5.40 from $4.50, while B200 will climb 19% to $8.50 from $7.15. The largest increase applies to the B300, with rates rising 21% to $9.50 per GPU-hour from $7.85.

CPU-only compute services also face increases. AMD EPYC Genoa CPU rates will rise 25% to $0.015 per vCPU-hour from $0.012, while Genoa memory increases 41% to $0.0045 per GiB-hour from $0.0032. The ultimate impact on customer bills depends on their specific configurations and usage patterns.

The timing reflects robust demand for AI infrastructure. In July, Nebius secured approximately $775 million in debt financing backed by deployed GPU infrastructure and contracted customer cash flows. Last month, the company reported Q2 revenue of $582.3 million, a 454% increase year-over-year, driven by AI Cloud revenue surging 514% to $574.9 million. Adjusted EBITDA swung to a $236.2 million profit from a $21 million loss a year earlier.

Management reaffirmed guidance for $3 billion to $3.4 billion in 2026 revenue and expects to achieve $7 billion to $9 billion in annual recurring revenue by year-end. Morningstar analysts noted that higher GPU spot prices driving higher-priced contracts would significantly improve profitability in late 2026 and 2027.

results.title: Huurprijs voor Europese GPU-capaciteit stijgt tot 21 procent - MSP Business
highlights:
Nebius verhoogt per 1 oktober 2026 zijn uurprijzen voor het huren van GPU-capaciteit met 17 tot 21 procent. Dat blijkt uit de maandelijkse Europese GPU-prijsindex van onderzoeksbureau Lindstead. Volgens dezelfde index huur je een NVIDIA H100 bij Europese aanbieders nog steeds voor ongeveer de helft van de prijs bij AWS en Microsoft Azure.

De prijsverhoging bij het in Amsterdam gevestigde Nebius geldt voor meerdere GPU-generaties. Een NVIDIA H100 gaat van ongeveer €3,38 naar €3,95 per uur ($3,85 naar $4,50). Voor de B300, de nieuwste generatie, stijgt het uurtarief van ongeveer €6,88 naar €8,33 ($7,85 naar $9,50).

Lindstead plaatst de verhoging in een bredere ontwikkeling. Volgens het bureau is de mediane huurprijs van een H200 in twaalf maanden met ongeveer 25 procent gestegen. Daarnaast constateert Lindstead dat elke nieuwe GPU-generatie per uur duurder is dan de vorige.

### Europese aanbieders onder hyperscalerprijzen

Uit de index blijkt dat Europese aanbieders een H100 op on-demandbasis verhuren voor ongeveer de helft van de prijs bij AWS en Microsoft Azure, en voor ongeveer een derde van het tarief bij Google Cloud. Het Franse OVHcloud rekent volgens de index ongeveer €2,62 per uur, het Finse Verda €3,09 en Nebius vanaf 1 oktober €3,95. Scaleway uit Frankrijk vermeldt prijzen vanaf €2,73 per uur.

Bij de Amerikaanse hyperscalers liggen de uurtarieven voor een H100 hoger. AWS rekent €6,03, Microsoft Azure €6,12 en Google Cloud €9,71 per uur.

Lindstead baseert de cijfers op de prijspagina’s van de aanbieders en op getdeploying.com, geraadpleegd op 27 september 2026. Dollarprijzen zijn omgerekend tegen de ECB-referentiekoers van 25 september 2026 (1 euro = 1,1403 dollar). De vergelijking betreft openbare on-demandprijzen. Tarieven bij reserveringen, langlopende contracten of maatwerkafspraken kunnen afwijken.

...

De Europese GPU-prijsindex vergelijkt maandelijks de openbare on-demandprijzen van Europese en Amerikaanse cloudaanbieders voor de NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 en B300. Per aanbieder vermeldt de index ook het hoofdkantoor en de eigenaar. Lindstead geeft aan geen commissies van aanbieders te ontvangen.

results.title: AWS reportedly lifts GPU capacity prices again, with a 15% hike flagged for October 7
highlights:
Amazon Web Services may be raising prices on its reserved GPU compute yet again. A post on X claims AWS is lifting reserved compute prices for a fourth quarter, with a 15% increase set to begin October 7.

## What AWS has actually raised in 2026

The increases center on EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML. That product lets customers lock in GPU capacity for machine learning workloads ahead of time.

The first confirmed move came in January 2026. AWS raised Capacity Block prices by approximately 15%, with the hike landing on instances that run NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

A second, larger bump followed on July 1, 2026. That one added roughly 20% to the same GPU capacity service.

The effect shows up clearly on a single machine. After the July change, the H200-based p5e.48xlarge instance went from about $34.61 per hour to about $39 per hour in most regions. In the US West region, the post-July price for that instance reached $49.74 per hour.

The October 7 increase is a different story. The 15% figure comes from the X post, and research findings indicate that number has not been publicly confirmed by AWS.

...

AWS has reportedly framed these changes as a response to supply and demand.

The scope of the increases is narrow on purpose. They hit reserved capacity carved out for GPU workloads, not standard on-demand instances or general Reserved Instances.

Capacity Blocks let customers book GPU capacity up to eight weeks ahead of time. The reservations can also be shared across accounts, which helps larger organizations spread capacity between teams.

...

The most direct impact falls on companies that rely on reserved GPU blocks for AI training and inference. If the reported October 7 increase does take effect, it would stack on top of the January and July hikes. Each new percentage lands on an already higher base, so the cumulative squeeze grows faster than the individual numbers suggest.

Regional gaps add another wrinkle. The spread between roughly $39 per hour in most regions and $49.74 per hour in US West is wide enough that workload placement becomes a real cost decision, not just a latency one.

results.title: GPU rental prices in 2026: what moved and why — Strata GPU
highlights:
H100 rates fell to $1.70 an hour in late 2025 and climbed back above $3 by September 2026. What that swing means for anyone buying compute.

Few prices in technology moved as much as GPU rental rates over the last three years. Understanding the cycle helps you decide when to lock in a rate and when to stay flexible.

## 2023–2024: scarcity

After ChatGPT, demand for H100s outran supply. Hyperscaler on-demand rates sat around $7–8 per GPU-hour and lead times for clusters ran to months.

## 2024–2025: the glut

New datacenters came online, and many buyers who had reserved capacity found they needed less of it. Marketplace rates fell steadily, and one-year contract prices reached a low of about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025, according to SemiAnalysis.

## 2026: tight again

Inference and media-generation demand absorbed the surplus faster than expected. By March 2026 roughly half of providers had no on-demand H100 stock, and capacity coming online through the summer was booked in advance. The Silicon Data H100 rental index stood at $3.06 in September 2026.

## What it means for buyers

- Lock rates for steady workloads. When the market is tight, a reservation buys availability as much as a discount.
- Keep bursts flexible. On-demand capacity for experiments avoids committing at the top of a cycle.
- Don't buy hardware to escape the cycle. Owners of GPUs bought in 2023 watched their rental value fall by about three quarters before it recovered.

results.title: Nvidia manufactures the chip nearly every AI cloud provider is built on. Nvidia's own cloud product, DGX Cloud, has no public rate card, no pricing page, and no self-serve checkout. | Compute Stacker
highlights:
Nvidia manufactures the chip nearly every AI cloud provider is built on. Nvidia's own cloud product, DGX Cloud, has no public rate card, no pricing page, and no self-serve checkout.

We checked. There's no number to find before you talk to a sales rep.

Compare that to every other major provider we track: CoreWeave publishes $6.16/GPU-hour for H100. Nebius publishes $3.85. Lambda publishes $3.99. All three numbers are sitting on a public page, verifiable, comparable, no phone call required.

That gap isn't an oversight. A published rate card is a ceiling, it caps what a provider can charge and gives customers something to negotiate against. Sales-negotiated pricing has no ceiling and no floor. It moves per customer, per volume commitment, per how much leverage someone walks into the conversation with. Nvidia can quote a startup one number and a frontier lab an entirely different one, and neither ever finds out what the other paid.

results.title: Best AI & GPU Hosting 2026: RunPod, DigitalOcean, Lambda and CoreWeave Compared | HostCompareHub
highlights:
Editor's note — GPU list prices change weekly and flagship cards sell out. Every rate on this page is the provider's published on-demand list price on our verification date (September 2026), excluding tax, and is included as a like-for-like starting point rather than a live quote. Confirm availability and current rates in the provider console before you commit a training run.

## RunPod leads — per-second billing, published rates and a GPU catalogue that spans consumer cards to B300

AI workloads are spiky, and the platforms that win are the ones that stop charging when the job stops. RunPod publishes self-serve rates with no quota request between you and a running GPU, bills per second on Pods and Serverless, charges nothing for egress, and prices everything from an RTX A5000 at $0.27/hr to a B300 at $7.89/hr — so a small model never pays for 80 GB of HBM it cannot use. DigitalOcean is the strongest pick for teams already on its control plane, Lambda is the reserved-cluster specialist, and Vast.ai is the cheapest headline rate if the workload can survive an interruption.

...

- The headline rate is not the bill — storage, egress and idle time are separate lines. A powered-off DigitalOcean GPU Droplet still bills, because the disk, RAM and IP stay reserved.
- Billing rounding is a real tax — a job that finishes at 6h04m bills as seven hours on an hourly-rounding provider. Prefer per-second where your jobs are short.
- Marketplaces are not clouds — on Vast.ai the host sets price, storage persistence and transfer cost. There is no platform SLA, and interruptible offers can be reclaimed at any time.
- Flagships sell out — B200 and B300 supply is tight through 2026. The cheapest listed rate is worth nothing if the card is unavailable when your run starts.
- Serverless active hours cost more — scale-to-zero is genuinely free when idle, but the per-active-hour rate sits above a dedicated on-demand instance. You are buying elasticity, not the lowest sticker.

...

## Start on DigitalOcean GPU Droplets

Our pick for teams already running on DigitalOcean: H100 and H200 GPU Droplets from $4.41 and $4.47 per GPU-hour on-demand, the widest AMD Instinct range on this list, managed databases and Spaces in the same account, and per-second billing with a five-minute minimum. Reserve for 12 months and H100 drops to $3.26 per GPU-hour. Confirm current GPU availability and egress at checkout — powered-off Droplets continue to bill.

...

| Provider | Best for | Strength | Tradeoff | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod | Most teams, from prototyping to production inference | Per-second billing on Pods and Serverless, published self-serve rates, no egress fees, A5000 $0.27/hr to B300 $7.89/hr | Community Cloud has no SLA; Serverless active hours cost more than on-demand | 4.7 |
| DigitalOcean | Teams already inside the DO control plane | H100 $4.41 and H200 $4.47 per GPU-hour, widest AMD MI300X–MI355X range, managed DBs and Spaces in one account | Powered-off GPU Droplets still bill; no scale-to-zero; H100 above RunPod | 4.6 |
| Lambda | Reserved multi-node training at cluster scale | 1-Click Clusters 16–2,000+ GPUs with InfiniBand, Lambda Stack, H100 $6.16→$5.54 per GPU-hour by size | Per-minute billing, no serverless, no published spot tier, rate excludes tax | 4.5 |
| CoreWeave | Kubernetes-native clusters and enterprise AI | Node-level H100 $49.24/hr (=$6.16/GPU), H200 $50.44, B200 $68.80; InfiniBand, ClusterMAX Platinum | Priced per 8-GPU node — high entry point, sales-led, no single-GPU experiments | 4.4 |
| Vast.ai | Fault-tolerant batch jobs and cheap fine-tuning | Marketplace floor H100 SXM ~$1.49–1.73/hr, RTX 4090 from ~$0.13/hr, per-second billing | No platform SLA; host sets storage, transfer and persistence; interruptible can be reclaimed | 4.3 |
| Modal | Serverless inference that scales to zero | Per-second billing on active time only, Python-native deployment, idle costs nothing | Vendor-specific programming model, cold starts, active-hour rate above dedicated | 4.2 |
| Hostinger VPS | A cheap always-on box for a small self-hosted model | KVM VPS with NVMe and root from a few dollars a month for CPU-only serving or orchestration | No GPU on standard plans; intro→renewal jump; not for training | 4.1 |
| Contabo | Cheap persistent storage next to a rented GPU | Very low per-GB and per-core pricing on 24-month terms; good for datasets and preprocessing | No on-demand GPU inventory; term commitment for promo pricing; support window | 4.0 |

Pricing model varies by provider and is not comparable column-for-column: RunPod, Vast.ai, DigitalOcean and Modal bill per second (Modal on active time only); Lambda bills per minute; CoreWeave bills per hour per 8-GPU node; Hostinger VPS and Contabo are term-promo subscriptions. No provider here uses a shared-hosting style introductory-then-renewal doubling.

...

### The unit of comparison is the GPU-hour, not the month

Web hosting is priced per month because a website runs all month. An AI workload does not. A fine-tuning run might occupy eight H100s for two days and then vanish; an inference endpoint might idle at zero and burst to a dozen requests a second. That is why every serious GPU platform prices per hour or finer, and why a "monthly equivalent" is only meaningful once you multiply by the hours you will actually run. The published rate per GPU-hour is the honest number, and it is the one we compare.

Two providers selling the same H100 can differ two to three times. On published self-serve rates in September 2026, an H100 SXM runs about $3.49 per GPU-hour on RunPod Secure Cloud, $3.99–4.29 on Lambda, $4.41 on DigitalOcean, and roughly $6.16 per GPU on CoreWeave once you divide its node price by eight. The marketplace floor on Vast.ai is far lower again, near $1.49–1.73, and a Community Cloud host on RunPod can undercut the platform's own Secure tier. The differences are large enough that the choice of provider, not the choice of model, is often the biggest line in a training budget.

...

Per-second billing against per-hour billing is not a rounding detail on bursty work. A job that finishes at six hours and four minutes costs six hours and four minutes on RunPod, DigitalOcean, Vast.ai or Modal — and seven hours on any provider that rounds up to the next billable hour. Run a hundred short evaluation jobs a month and the difference is an entire extra day of GPU time you never used. Lambda bills per minute and CoreWeave per hour at node level; that is a deliberate simplification for long cluster runs, and the wrong shape for a notebook that starts and stops all afternoon.

The finer question is what you are billed for when nothing is running. DigitalOcean bills you for a powered-off GPU Droplet, because the disk, RAM, CPU and IP address remain reserved — a fact worth knowing before you park an H100 overnight. Modal and RunPod Serverless go the other way and charge for active time or active workers only, which is exactly the trade that makes scale-to-zero worth its higher active-hour rate. Neither model is wrong; they answer different questions, and the honest comparison names which one you are buying.

...

RunPod is the balanced default. Its catalogue spans an RTX A5000 at $0.27 per hour to a B300 at $7.89, its rates are published and self-serve, its Serverless tier scales to zero, and it charges no egress. The split between Community and Secure Cloud is the honest part: Community is cheaper and carries no SLA, Secure is vetted data centres with a formal guarantee. Read the tier before you read the price.

DigitalOcean is the pick if your stack already lives there. H100 and H200 GPU Droplets at $4.41 and $4.47 per GPU-hour sit above the cheapest specialists, but they arrive inside the same control plane as your databases, Spaces buckets and VPC, with per-second billing and a five-minute minimum — and the widest AMD Instinct range here, from MI300X through MI355X. Just remember the powered-off rule.

Lambda is the reserved-cluster specialist. Its on-demand rates are competitive rather than cheapest, but its 1-Click Clusters run from 16 to 2,000-plus GPUs over InfiniBand with rates that fall as the cluster grows, from $6.16 per GPU-hour at 16 H100s to $5.54 at 256. Lambda Stack keeps drivers and frameworks in sync, which is worth real money if environment drift is your recurring pain. There is no serverless product, so inference means running your own stack.

CoreWeave sells Kubernetes at cluster scale, and its rate card must be read carefully: prices are per eight-GPU node, not per GPU. An HGX H100 node is $49.24 per hour, which is $6.16 per GPU — quote the node figure beside a competitor's per-GPU rate and you overstate CoreWeave eightfold. For the enterprise that wants managed Kubernetes, InfiniBand and a supplier that has earned SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX Platinum three times running, the premium is deliberate. For a single-GPU experiment, it is the wrong product.

Vast.ai is a marketplace, not a cloud, and it is the cheapest headline rate in the category. H100 SXM listings appear near $1.49–1.73 an hour and A100 80 GB below a dollar. The catch is structural rather than incidental: the host sets the price, the storage persistence, the transfer cost and the data location, there is no platform SLA, and interruptible offers can be reclaimed when a higher bidder arrives. Independent analyses recommend budgeting twenty to forty per cent above the lowest listed rate for realistic planning. Great for a checkpointed fine-tune; wrong for a production endpoint.

...

GPU cloud rents you GPU time by the hour or second and you stop paying when you stop; a dedicated GPU server is a flat monthly rate for a machine committed to you. Cloud wins for short experiments, bursty inference and workloads that genuinely need to scale up and down. A dedicated monthly server typically becomes cheaper once you are running past roughly eighteen hours a day, and it removes the cold-start and reclamation risk that the cheapest cloud tiers carry. If your workload is steady and long, price the monthly option before defaulting to hourly.

...

Always convert to the same unit, and treat the lowest rate as the

...

Per-unit capacity has generally become cheaper over time, but list rates for a given card move in both directions with supply, and the newest generation carries a premium that only erodes as the next one ships. What has been stable is the direction of the market: more providers, finer billing granularity and more serverless options each generation. Because rates change weekly, the only safe practice is to treat any published number — including the ones in this guide — as a dated reference point and confirm it in the provider console before you start a run.

results.title: AI Server Cost: Buy, Rent by the Hour or Rent Dedicated?
highlights:
## What Renting by the Hour Actually Costs

Renting GPU compute by the hour has no single price, current H100 rates span roughly $1.99 to $14 per GPU-hour depending on the provider, region, and how much capacity guarantee you’re paying for. RunPod, one of the more accessible self-serve platforms, lists H100 PCIe from $1.99 per GPU-hour and H100 SXM at $2.69, billed by the second with no long-term commitment.

That range exists because you are not just buying compute, you are buying a specific combination of reliability, region, and contract length, and providers price each combination differently. The range has also moved substantially in one direction: H100 rental rates fell an estimated 64 to 75 percent between late 2024 and early 2026 as new GPU cloud providers entered the market and competition intensified. A rate that made sense to quote a year ago may already be well above what the same hardware costs today.

Hourly billing earns its cost specifically for short, bursty, or unpredictable workloads, a training run measured in days, an experiment that might not continue past this week, a workload where committing to a month makes no sense yet.

...

A dedicated GPU server billed monthly gives you exclusive, always-on access to the hardware for a fixed price, and for workloads that run near-continuously, that fixed price frequently beats the equivalent hourly cost. GPU Cloud HQ illustrates the gap directly: a dedicated H100 SXM runs $1,249 per month on a committed plan, against roughly $2,446 for the same GPU run for 730 hours at their market-median on-demand rate. Renting the identical hardware by the hour, continuously, costs very close to double what renting it dedicated costs.

...

| Billing model | H100 SXM, running continuously |
| --- | --- |
| Hourly, on-demand (730 hrs) | ≈ $2,446/month |
| Dedicated, committed monthly | $1,249/month |

...

H100 rental rates fell an estimated 64 to 75 percent between late 2024 and early 2026, driven largely by a wave of new GPU cloud providers entering the market and competing on price.
